EMPLOYER USE OF CONSUMER CREDIT REPORTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Labor Code § 1024.5, a statute that restricts whether Acme Innovations LLC may use a consumer credit report to make an employment decision about Jordan Lee regarding the position of Software Engineer — a different, and more specific, restriction than California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA), Civil Code §§ 1786 et seq., addressed elsewhere in this corpus. ICRAA governs the disclosure, authorization, agency-certification, and adverse-action mechanics an employer must follow when it seeks to obtain an investigative consumer report — a report on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living. Labor Code § 1024.5 addresses a different, threshold question that does not turn on any of ICRAA's disclosure steps: whether an employer may use an ordinary credit-based consumer credit report — a report concerning a person's credit worthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity — to make most employment decisions at all, regardless of what disclosure or authorization the employer has obtained, unless the position at issue falls within one of a specific statutory list of exceptions. This document states facts about what § 1024.5 says: its core prohibition, its statutory list of exempted positions, its own definitions, an exclusion it states for certain financial institutions, and how the statute is enforced. It does not determine, and does not tell Acme Innovations LLC or Jordan Lee, whether the position of Software Engineer falls within any exception, whether Acme Innovations LLC's use of a consumer credit report for that position is lawful, or what either party should do about any particular use of a consumer credit report.

THE CORE PROHIBITION: CONSUMER CREDIT REPORTS RESTRICTED TO LISTED POSITIONS
California Labor Code § 1024.5(a) states that an employer or prospective employer shall not use a consumer credit report for employment purposes unless the position of the person for whom the report is sought falls within one of the categories the statute itself lists. By its own terms, the prohibition is written as a default rule against using a consumer credit report for employment purposes, with the statute's list of categories operating as its own stated exceptions — the statute introduces that list with the phrase "is any of the following," rather than offering the list as illustrative examples.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer or prospective employer shall not use a consumer credit report for employment purposes unless the position of the person for whom the report is sought is any of the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), core prohibition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1024.5.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the statute's opening prohibition; the list of exempted categories the prohibition refers to is addressed in a separate clause below rather than repeated here. The statute does not itself define the word "use," and this document does not address whether obtaining, requesting, or merely possessing a consumer credit report — as distinct from using one to make an employment decision — falls within the prohibition. Only one source is cited for this clause, since it states a single provision's opening sentence rather than combining multiple sources.

THE STATUTORY LIST OF EXEMPTED POSITIONS
Labor Code § 1024.5(a) lists eight categories of position for which an employer may use a consumer credit report for employment purposes: (1) a managerial position (a term the statute separately defines); (2) a position in the state Department of Justice; (3) that of a sworn peace officer or other law enforcement position; (4) a position for which the information contained in the report is required by law to be disclosed or obtained; (5) a position that involves regular access — for any purpose other than the routine solicitation and processing of credit card applications in a retail establishment — to all three of a single person's bank or credit card account information, Social Security number, and date of birth; (6) a position in which the person is, or would be, a named signatory on the employer's bank or credit card account, authorized to transfer money on the employer's behalf, or authorized to enter into financial contracts on the employer's behalf; (7) a position that involves access to confidential or proprietary information — including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, process, or trade secret — meeting the statute's own two-part description of independent economic value from secrecy and a reasonable effort to maintain that secrecy; and (8) a position that involves regular access to cash totaling ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or more of the employer, a customer, or client, during the workday.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(1) A managerial position. (2) A position in the state Department of Justice. (3) That of a sworn peace officer or other law enforcement position. (4) A position for which the information contained in the report is required by law to be disclosed or obtained. (5) A position that involves regular access, for any purpose other than the routine solicitation and processing of credit card applications in a retail establishment, to all of the following types of information of any one person: (A) Bank or credit card account information. (B) Social security number. (C) Date of birth. (6) A position in which the person is, or would be, any of the following: (A) A named signatory on the bank or credit card account of the employer. (B) Authorized to transfer money on behalf of the employer. (C) Authorized to enter into financial contracts on behalf of the employer. (7) A position that involves access to confidential or proprietary information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, process or trade secret that (i) derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable by proper means by, other persons who may obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information, and (ii) is the subject of an effort that is reasonable under the circumstances to maintain secrecy of the information. (8) A position that involves regular access to cash totaling ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or more of the employer, a customer, or client, during the workday."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(a)(1)-(8) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), list of exempted positions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1024.5.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statutory list as written; it does not determine whether the duties of the position at issue fall within any category, and does not address how a court or agency would apply an undefined term the statute uses — such as "regular access" in categories (5) and (8), or the scope of "confidential or proprietary information" in category (7) beyond the statute's own two-part description. The definition of "managerial position" referenced in category (1) is addressed in a separate clause below rather than repeated here. Only one source is cited, since the entire list comes from a single subdivision of a single statutory section.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: "CONSUMER CREDIT REPORT" AND "MANAGERIAL POSITION"
Labor Code § 1024.5(c) defines two terms the statute uses. First, "consumer credit report" is defined to have the same meaning given in Civil Code § 1785.3(c) — a definition from California's separate Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act (CCRAA) — except that § 1024.5's own definition excludes a report that both verifies income or employment and does not include credit-related information, such as credit history, credit score, or credit record. Civil Code § 1785.3(c) itself defines "consumer credit report" broadly: any written, oral, or other communication of information by a consumer credit reporting agency bearing on a person's credit worthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity, used or expected to be used (among other listed purposes) as a factor in establishing a person's eligibility for employment purposes. Second, § 1024.5(c) defines "managerial position" — the first category on the exempted-positions list — as an employee covered by the executive exemption set forth in Wage Order 4 of the Industrial Welfare Commission, codified at 8 California Code of Regulations § 11040.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(1) “Consumer credit report” has the same meaning as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1785.3 of the Civil Code, but does not include a report that (A) verifies income or employment, and (B) does not include credit-related information, such as credit history, credit score, or credit record."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), definition of "consumer credit report" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1024.5.)
  "(2) “Managerial position” means an employee covered by the executive exemption set forth in subparagraph (1) of paragraph (A) of Section 1 of Wage Order 4 of the Industrial Welfare Commission (8 Cal. Code Regs. 11040)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), definition of "managerial position" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1024.5.)
  "“Consumer credit report” means any written, oral, or other communication of any information by a consumer credit reporting agency bearing on a consumer’s credit worthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity, which is used or is expected to be used, or collected in whole or in part, for the purpose of serving as a factor in establishing the consumer’s eligibility for: (1) credit to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, or (2) employment purposes, or (3) hiring of a dwelling unit, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1940, or (4) other purposes authorized in Section 1785.11."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1785.3(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act, definition of "consumer credit report" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1785.3.)
  Known gap: The Civil Code § 1785.3(c) citation below is not independent corroboration of the Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(1) citation — § 1024.5(c)(1) expressly adopts the Civil Code definition by cross-reference, so the two citations describe the same defined term at its point of origin (Civil Code § 1785.3(c)) and at the statute that adopts it by reference (Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(1)), not two independently corroborating sources. The two Labor Code citations below, § 1024.5(c)(1) and § 1024.5(c)(2), are likewise subdivisions of the same statutory section, not independent sources. This document did not independently fetch or verify the text of Wage Order 4 of the Industrial Welfare Commission or 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 11040 themselves, which § 1024.5(c)(2) cross-references for the "executive exemption" that in turn defines "managerial position" — that regulatory text is not quoted or restated here. Civil Code § 1785.3(c) also lists several categories of report its own text excludes from the CCRAA's "consumer credit report" definition (for example, certain internal-organization communications, and reports based on personal interviews about character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living) that are not restated in this clause.

EXCLUSION FOR CERTAIN FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS SUBJECT TO FEDERAL PRIVACY LAW
Labor Code § 1024.5(b) states that the section does not apply to a person or business subject to 15 U.S.C. §§ 6801-6809 — provisions of the federal Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act — and to state and federal statutes or regulations implementing those sections, if that person or business is subject to compliance oversight by a state or federal regulatory agency with respect to those laws.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) This section does not apply to a person or business subject to Sections 6801 to 6809, inclusive, of Title 15 of the United States Code and state and federal statutes or regulations implementing those sections if the person or business is subject to compliance oversight by a state or federal regulatory agency with respect to those laws."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), financial-institution exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1024.5.)
  Known gap: This document did not independently fetch or verify the text of 15 U.S.C. §§ 6801-6809 themselves, nor did it identify which state or federal regulatory agencies exercise the "compliance oversight" the statute refers to, or which categories of person or business are, in fact, subject to that oversight. Only Labor Code § 1024.5(b) itself is cited below; this clause does not identify, and does not determine, whether the employer at issue is a person or business within this exclusion's scope.

ENFORCEMENT: NO SECTION-SPECIFIC REMEDY STATED; GENERAL PAGA MECHANISM
Labor Code § 1024.5 does not itself state a private right of action, a specific civil penalty, or any other enforcement mechanism for a violation of its terms — unlike, for example, ICRAA's own civil-liability provision addressed in this corpus's ICRAA document. Separately, the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act of 2004 (PAGA), Labor Code §§ 2698-2699.8, states that any provision of the Labor Code that provides for a civil penalty to be assessed and collected by the state Labor and Workforce Development Agency may, as an alternative, be recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of themselves and other current or former employees, following the procedures the statute specifies. For a Labor Code provision that does not itself specify a civil penalty, Labor Code § 2699(f) establishes a default civil penalty structure: five hundred dollars for a violation where the person does not, at the time of the alleged violation, employ one or more employees, or, where the person does employ one or more employees, one hundred dollars for each aggrieved employee per pay period, subject to exceptions the statute states for certain other, unrelated Labor Code provisions not addressed in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any provision of this code that provides for a civil penalty to be assessed and collected by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or any of its departments, divisions, commissions, boards, agencies, or employees, for a violation of this code, may, as an alternative, be recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of the employee and other current or former employees against whom a violation of the same provision was committed pursuant to the procedures specified in Section 2699.3."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Private Attorneys General Act of 2004, civil-action alternative to agency-collected civil penalties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.)
  "For all provisions of this code except those for which a civil penalty is specifically provided, there is established a civil penalty for a violation of these provisions, as follows: (1) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person does not employ one or more employees, the civil penalty is five hundred dollars ($500). (2) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person employs one or more employees, the civil penalty is as follows: (A) One hundred dollars ($100) for each aggrieved employee per pay period, except that:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Private Attorneys General Act of 2004, default civil penalty for provisions without a specified penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general PAGA enforcement framework as its own text describes it; it does not determine that a court would in fact apply PAGA's default civil penalty to a Labor Code § 1024.5 violation specifically, and no source located in this research discusses PAGA's application to § 1024.5 by name. This document does not address PAGA's separate requirement that an aggrieved employee give notice to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency before filing a civil action (Labor Code § 2699.3), which was not independently fetched or verified here, and it does not address whether a remedy for a § 1024.5 violation might also be available under some other law, such as California's Unfair Competition Law — this document did not research that possibility. The two citations below, Labor Code § 2699(a) and § 2699(f), are both subdivisions of the same statutory section, so they corroborate PAGA's own internal structure rather than serving as two independent sources; neither is independent of Labor Code § 1024.5 either, since § 1024.5's own text says nothing about PAGA — this clause connects the two based on the plain terms of § 2699(f) ("[f]or all provisions of this code except those for which a civil penalty is specifically provided"), not on any source that discusses § 1024.5's enforcement specifically.
